UNSC condemns Swat suicide blast after Pakistan sounds alarm on Afghan terrorist havens. UNITED NATIONS: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) on Thursday strongly condemned the suicide bombing in Swat last week, calling it a “heinous and cowardly” terrorist attack after Pakistan warned the body that multiple terrorist groups continue to operate from safe havens inside Afghanistan. In a press statement issued by the Office of the UN secretary general’s spokesperson, the council said it condemned “in the strongest terms” the “heinous and cowardly” suicide attack outside the police station in Swat’s Kabal on Aug 2. “This reprehensible act of terrorism resulted in the grievous loss of at least 16 Pakistani nationals, mostly civilians, and injuries to dozens of others. Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) has claimed responsibility for this terrorist attack,” it added. The UNSC also expressed solidarity with Pakistan, saying, “The members of the Security Council express their deepest sympathy and condolences to the families of the victims and to the government and the people of Pakistan, and wish a speedy and full recovery to those who were injured.” The statement reaffirmed the international body’s longstanding position that terrorism “in all its forms and manifestations constitutes one of the most serious threats to international peace and security”. It further stressed the importance of bringing those responsible to justice, declaring: “The members of the council underlined the need to hold perpetrators, organisers, financiers and sponsors of these reprehensible acts of terrorism accountable and bring them to justice.” They urged all UN member states, in accordance with their obligations under international law and relevant UNSC resolutions, to cooperate actively with the government of Pakistan in this regard. The council also reiterated that “any acts of terrorism are criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, wherever, whenever and by whomsoever committed” and reaffirmed that all countries must combat terrorism in accordance with the UN Charter and international law, including international human rights, refugee and humanitarian law. Earlier this week, Pakistan told a UNSC meeting that several terrorist organisations continue to operate from sanctuaries inside Afghanistan, posing an increasing threat to regional and international security. Addressing a briefing on threats to international peace and security caused by terrorism, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Asim Iftikhar, said the country continued to face a grave terrorist threat emanating from across its western border. He identified the banned TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and its Majeed Brigade, the Islamic State Khorasan (IS-K) and its affiliates, the East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM), and Al Qaeda affiliates as groups that, according to Pakistan, maintain safe havens inside Afghanistan. Pakistan urged the international community to ensure that Afghan territory is not used by terrorist organisations to launch attacks against neighbouring countries and called for stronger international cooperation against cross-border terrorism. The developments also followed the fourth US-Pakistan Counterterrorism Dialogue held in Washington on Tuesday, where officials from both countries reaffirmed their commitment to combating terrorist organisations.

Trump signs orders to limit US birthright citizenship, despite Supreme Court ruling. US President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday in a new but narrower attempt to curtail birthright citizenship, once again challenging a provision of the US Constitution even though the Supreme Court rejected his previous effort. Limiting birthright citizenship has been one of the top priorities in the Republican president’s crackdown on immigration, with the White House taking particular aim at what it calls “birth tourism,” in which pregnant foreigners travel to the US to give birth. After his June 30 setback in the Supreme Court, Trump called on Congress to act, but on Thursday he opted for executive orders, which set policy but do not carry the same weight as laws passed by Congress. The Supreme Court had struck down as unconstitutional Trump’s earlier executive order , which targeted a wide swath of immigrants in the country illegally or temporarily. The administration argues the new directive falls outside the purview of the Supreme Court ruling, as it seeks to reinterpret the narrow, historical exceptions to citizenship at birth and expand who is ineligible. “That practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the Thursday signing ceremony in the Oval Office. The Centre for Immigration Studies, which supports lower levels of immigration, estimated in an analysis in 2020 that between 20,000 and 25,000 mothers came to the US for birth tourism in a year-long period between 2016 and 2017. There were 3.6 million births in the US in 2025. The executive orders also limit the rights of children born to foreign government employees in the US and children of people who are classified as alien enemies. The orders could also affect people born in US territories, should Congress enact a proposed law to end automatic citizenship there. Trump’s new orders are likely to face legal challenge. Legal experts said it was unclear what effect the executive orders might have given the Supreme Court ruling, while immigrant advocates called it an attempt to evade the high court’s decision. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) predicted it was doomed to fail in court. “Just five weeks ago, the Supreme Court made clear that birthright citizenship is not subject to a president’s whims; it is a constitutional guarantee that has stood for more than 150 years. Today’s executive orders are nothing more than an attempt to get around that ruling,” said Deborah Fleischaker, a former Biden administration official who is now with UnidosUS, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organisation. Zain Lakhani of the Women’s Refugee Commission said the executive orders could trample the rights of pregnant women seeking lawful entry “in one of the most vulnerable moments of their lives”, and called on the government to establish guidelines honouring the Supreme Court ruling. ‘A very unfortunate decision’ Trump, speaking in the Oval Office on Thursday, called the Supreme Court’s 6-3 ruling on June 30 a “very unfortunate decision”, decrying that “people are building businesses around” birth tourism. “That’s not the way it’s supposed to work. It’s a disgrace. They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen,” he said. Trump’s prior executive order, issued on his first day in office in 2025 as part of a suite of policies to crack down on immigration, directed US agencies not to recognise the citizenship of children born in the United States if neither parent is an American citizen or legal permanent resident, also called a “green card” holder — barring babies of immigrants in the US illegally or temporarily. The 14th Amendment has long been interpreted as guaranteeing citizenship for babies born in the US with only narrow exceptions such as the children of foreign diplomats or members of an enemy occupying force. “This was done for a different reason. This was done right after the Civil War. This was for the babies of slaves, and what’s happening now?” Trump said. There are no official figures tallying the number of foreigners who come to the US for the explicit purpose of giving birth and obtaining citizenship for their children, or the cost to taxpayers. In any case, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in the Supreme Court ruling that the authors of the 14th Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in the land. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community. We keep that promise today,” Roberts wrote. The 14th Amendment provision known as the Citizenship Clause states: “All persons born or naturalised in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens of the United States and of the state wherein they reside.”

Exhumation of Mir Raza Ali's body postponed after family objects to abrupt reconstitution of medico-legal board. KARACHI: The exhumation of 25-year-old businessman and Institute of Business Administration graduate Mir Raza Ali’s body was postponed on Friday after his family objected to the abrupt reconstitution of the medico-legal board. Ali’s body was found in bushes in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he went missing on July 28. While his family is convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, investigators probing the incident continue to build their case around the possibility that he died by suicide. His family was present at the cemetery adjacent to Tariq Road’s Rehmania Masjid for the exhumation on Friday. But, the exhumation was deferred, with the counsel for Ali’s family, Jibran Nasir, telling the media that they had informed the investigating officer that the family had rejected the reconstituted board and would not accept an exhumation by it “under any circumstances”. Standing alongside Ali’s father, Mir Hussain Ali Khan, Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts and held the police, health ministry and the Sindh government responsible for the delay. The family could not allow the examination to be performed by members whose “qualifications and intentions were under question”, he added. He recalled that the previous night, Hyderabad health director general dismissed the original board and reconstituted it, adding four names from Hyderabad. Nasir claimed that following outcry over the reconstituted board, the DG health then issued a backdated notification at around 10am on Friday. “He says more members may be added [to the board], but the four chosen by him should also remain a part of it,” Nasir alleged. He added that they still had not been informed why the original board was reconstituted. Moreover, he continued, now there was another notification that authorised the Hyderabad health director general to form the medico-legal board, a power that previously rested with the Sindh health secretary. The authorities “needed to be given a lesson on law” as under the Sindh Medicolegal Act 2023, only a police surgeon had the complete authority in matters of exhumation, he said, adding that the act was a special law that prevailed over general laws. The lawyer said they would not be making any demands to the police. Ali’s father was now directly raising questions to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, he said. “We will also not turn to the Sindh inspector general of police (IG). What do you ask an IG who claims that the investigation has been completed even before the exhumation and medical examination?” He reasserted that they only trusted the original eight-member board, adding, “Sindh government, they were hired by you. And if they are not competent enough, then how were they appointed in the first place?” Nasir alleged that police were presenting the CCTV evidence “selectively” and demanded that all facts of the case be brought to light. He said CCTV footage shared showed a motorcycle and a trash picker passing by the body. But then, why did it not show the moment when Ali walked up to the place where his body was found, if he died by suicide, Nasir questioned. “Where did that footage go?” He added, “Why is it that people at the nearby guesthouse panicked and ran to a nearby property when Ali’s father inquired about him? […] And why were they not tracked?” Nasir further accused police of not letting Ali’s father see the complete CCTV footage. Concluding his talk, he said, “If not today, then maybe we will get the exhumation done tomorrow. We will try our best that the originally nominated doctors perform the examination, and I am sure the facts that they are going to such great lengths to bury will surface.” Speaking to reporters earlier in the day, the family’s counsel said that the Sindh Medicolegal Act 2023 required that if a magistrate issues an order for exhumation, the authority to form a board rested with the division’s police surgeon. “I believe I am standing in Karachi division where the police surgeon is Dr Summaiya Syed […] who would constitute the board and add forensic experts from the nearest possible public sector university,” Nasir said, questioning whether Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences was closer to Karachi than Dow Medical College or the Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC). Nasir alleged that the “illegal and dubious” board had no authority to examine the body. “We cannot allow them to disrespect the deceased and destroy evidence.” He also asked how a fresh notification was issued when the previous one had not yet been withdrawn, alleging that a third party and a “stranger” to the proceedings had intervened. “We will not accept any Plan C either,” he said, referring to the suggestion to merge the two boards. Earlier, he had also alleged on X that the Sindh government had “maliciously” changed the members of the board without any explanation. “The family expresses no consent for this new board and will not allow it to exhumate the body tomorrow morning and corrupt whatever evidence remains and it will be formally communicated to authorities,” he said, adding that the fresh notification would be challenged at the appropriate forum. ‘Malicious attempt to interfere with judicial proceedings’ Nasir also submitted a letter to the police surgeon on Friday, wherein he formally informed her of the family’s non-consent and stated that the reconstituted board was in “complete violation and negation” of the court’s order and had no legal basis. He held that it carried no binding value and was nothing “but a malicious attempt to interfere with judicial proceedings initiated by the court” and any directive in support of the board shall be viewed as a “further malicious attempt to provide cover to an illegal act and sabotage fair and transparent investigation”. Nasir said the family had not consented to the exhumation by the reconstituted board and warned that any attempt to proceed with the exhumation under the reconstituted medical board will be a violation of the dignity of the deceased, will put evidence at risk and will be a “blatant” contempt of court. He said the police surgeon that she remained “duty bound” to conduct the exhumation with the original medical board and further held that the action had “fortified the apprehension of our clients that instead of investigating the truth every effort is being made to suppress the truth and manipulate evidence and facts to arrive at a pre-determined outcome by the senior officers of police and the same is being done at behest of influentials who are being protected in the investigation into the death of Mir Raza Ali Khan”. He concluded that in case of any further proceedings through the “illegally constituted” board, the family had the right to approach the appropriate court and seek prosecution of the officers attempting to “jeopardise” the investigation. Reconstitution of board On Thursday, a Karachi court allowed the exhumation of Ali’s body on an application filed by Ali’s father, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medico-legal board for the exhumation of Ali’s body “at the earliest possible date and time”. The court ruling came after a controversy emerged between the Karachi police surgeon and investigators over alleged loopholes in the medico-legal report regarding the post-mortem examination. The Sindh health department then constituted the eight-member board, with Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed as the convener. Prof Dr Naseem Ahmed of Dow University of Health Sciences (DUHS), Dr Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Amir Hassan Khan of Citizens Police Liaison Committee, Additional Police Surgeon Dr Sirichand, Dr Kamran Khan and Dr Daniyal Mirza of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre and Dr Mohammed Yaseen, the admin in-charge of the police surgeon office, were the other members of the board. However, a new order has been issued by the Sindh health directorate general. The notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn , said that the board had been reconstituted to conduct the exhumation and medico-legal examination of the deceased. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new board, its members were changed to Prof Dr Zakiuddin from DUHS, Prof Dr Kazi Akbar and Prof Dr Abid Hussain Chang from Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences and Hyderabad Police Surgeon Dr Waseem Khan. Controversy over autopsy Raza, an IBA graduate and the owner of eatery Wafflix, had gone missing on July 28. The 25-year-old’s body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. Initially, on the complaint lodged by his father, a case was registered at the Ferozabad police station under Section 365 (kidnapping or abducting with intent secretly and wrongfully to confine a person) of the Pakistan Penal Code. Police maintain that the investigation has revealed that Ali had been facing financial difficulties and had asked his friends for money the night he died. According to police, he had left his home in PECHS Block-2 and hired a taxi through an app. The taxi driver dropped him a short distance from the spot where his body was found, police said. The case took a new turn when Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed told a private news channel on Tuesday that the postmortem findings of Ali’s body had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. She said the reported entry wound, bullet trajectory and exit wound did not correspond with one another. While it was scientifically possible for a bullet to enter through the back and exit from the front, she stressed that her assessment was based only on the postmortem report and photographs, as she had not examined the body herself. The police surgeon noted that entry wounds were typically smaller than exit wounds in firearm cases. She also said that gunshot residue, commonly found on the hands in suspected suicides, was not tested for in this case. Her interview prompted the police authorities to issue a statement, terming such observations as having the potential to adversely affect the ongoing investigation. The statement, however, said that exhumation of the dead body could be done on the medical board’s recommendation for further clarification by a committee of medico-legal experts with the court’s permission.

US to vet social media of foreign journalists applying for visas, report says. The US State Department will ​vet the social media accounts of foreign journalists applying for visas to work in the United ‌States, according to a media report on Thursday. The report in the conservative news outlet The Daily Signal cited an internal memo that said an initiative by President Donald Trump’s administration that requires applicants for many visa types to make their social media accounts public ​for screening was being expanded to include foreign media representatives. Applicants for another type of visa for ​workers from Canada and Mexico also will now be included in the screening, it said. The ⁠White House and the State Department’s official accounts on X shared a link to the article, but the ​State Department declined to confirm the specifics of the report, citing a policy of not commenting on “purported internal documents”. A ​State Department spokesperson said that what the department calls “online presence vetting” is used to ensure that applicants are eligible for a visa under US law. “The Department of State is screening and vetting to the maximum extent possible every foreign national seeking admission to ​the United States to ensure they will respect US law including the terms of their admission and do ​not pose a threat to US security, public safety or national interests,” the spokesperson said. “Officers use a variety of methods to ‌make ⁠informed decisions that protect national security, prevent fraud and ensure a thorough review of applicants,” the spokesperson added. It was unclear when the reported new policy would take effect. The Department of Homeland Security tightened rules last month around how long foreign journalists working in the United States, as well as other visa holders including foreign students, could remain in ​the country. It also builds ​on a series of ⁠ steps that Trump’s administration has taken since he began his second term in taking office in January 2025 to make online speech a factor in immigration and visa decisions. ​These steps have raised concerns among civil liberties advocates about freedom of speech. US Citizenship ​and Immigration Services ⁠has said it will screen the social media posts of immigrants and visa applicants, including for what it deems antisemitic content and “ anti-Americanism ”. The administration has canceled the visas of foreign students in the US who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism, ⁠in some cases attempting to ​deport those students. The State Department said in October 2025 that it ​revoked the visas of six foreign nationals over comments about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk , and said it would continue identifying visa ​holders it believed had celebrated the killing.

Bilawal claims 'certain elements' within PML-N are sowing division among allies, undermining PM Shehbaz. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari claimed on Friday that certain elements within the ruling PML-N were undermining Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and sowing discord between him and his political allies. The PPP and the PML-N have been engaged in a war of words since the latter emerged in the lead in Mirpur polls on July 27. The PML-N has also won the majority of the seats in the second phase , with the PPP accusing it of rigging and other violent tactics in both phases. The PPP chief was addressing an election rally in Azad Jammu and Kashmir’s Poonch district, where the third phase of elections in the region is slated to be held. “High-profile people are saying that the government has collapsed. I’m not saying that, nor am I casting doubt on the prime minister’s intentions. He’s a good man with good intentions. But what can he do when the people around him have bad intentions?” Bilawal asked. In reference to remarks he made earlier this week, the party chief highlighted that the PPP did not start the “countdown” to the government’s collapse, but rather these elements within the ruling party. “The PML-N’s fight is not with the PPP — it happens in elections, as it has before. The real fight is entirely different, because the PM, with his good intentions and actions, is undermined by a large part of the PML-N,” Bilawal alleged. “A big part of the PML-N wants the PM to fight not only the opposition, but also his own allies.” He then asked the audience: “Have there ever been elections held in six phases in Kashmir’s history? If Kashmir is one, then the election should have been held on a single day.” Bilawal said the elections were being held in phases “so that there is calm and the elections are peaceful, free and fair”, before asking: “But in which phase were the elections free, fair or peaceful?” “In truth, elections were carried out in phases so they could rig them. They knew that 10 seats were in their pocket from the start,” he alleged. “With the 10 seats in their pocket, they robbed Mirpur, they robbed Muzaffarabad, and they’re looking at you, in Poonch. They are looking at Bagh. On August 10, they will find out that those in Poonch and Bagh hunt tigers.” Elections are being held across AJK in three phases . Polls in Mirpur and Muzaffarabad divisions were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively. The first phase of polling in Mirpur saw the PML-N secure nine of the 13 seats while the PPP won the remaining four. In the second phase in Muzaffarabad, the PML-N bagged 15 more seats, while the PPP managed to add just six more to its tally. The third phase in Poonch division was set for August 10. Poonch Division comprises 11 constituencies — three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch and two in Sudhnoti district. However, earlier today, the AJK Election Commission revised the schedule for the third phase of elections in the region, saying polling would only be held in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts on August 10 amid concerns over the law and order situation. The electoral process in the constituencies of Poonch district and Sudhnoti’s Pallandri would not be held on August 10, the Election Commission said, adding that it reviewed the “current situation” regarding the scheduled elections in Poonch. It noted that according to a report it received from the AJK home secretary, there were “concerns over the law and order situation in some areas of Poonch district and Pallandri district”. The commission’s decision comes in the wake of clashes that took place between protesters and law enforcement personnel in Poonch district’s Rawalakot on July 27, which reportedly resulted in several casualties. Rawalakot has been gripped by unrest since early June , with the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) staging sit-ins periodically. The JAAC, which has been demanding the abolishment of 12 seats in the local legislature reserved for refugees from Indian-held Kashmir, has been holding protests in the region for several weeks now. The government has accused militant elements “pursuing a foreign agenda and backed by Indian funding” of fomenting the unrest.

Schedule for 3rd phase of AJK polls revised over law and order concerns. The Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Election Commission on Friday revised the schedule for the third phase of elections in the region, saying polling would only be held in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts on August 10 amid concerns over the law and order situation. Elections are being held across AJK in three phases amid tensions between protesters and the authorities. Polls in Mirpur and Muzaffarabad divisions were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively. The third phase in Poonch division was set for August 10. Poonch Division comprises 11 constituencies — three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch and two in Sudhnoti district. However, the Election Commission said in a press release on Friday that the electoral process will go ahead as planned on August 10 in only the division’s Bagh and Haveli districts. In its press release, the AJK Election Commission said polling will be held in the three constituencies of Bagh and one of Haveli on August 10 as per the previous schedule. However, the electoral process in the constituencies of Poonch district and Sudhnoti’s Pallandri will not be held on August 10, it said. The Election Commission said it reviewed the “current situation” regarding the scheduled elections in Poonch. It noted that according to a report it received from the AJK home secretary, there were “concerns over the law and order situation in some areas of Poonch district and Pallandri district”. “Moreover, the Election Commission received requests from some political personalities and candidates hailing from these districts, in which it has been requested to postpone the elections in Poonch district and Pallandri district considering the current situation,” the press release read. The electoral watchdog said it will announce the new polling dates and a revised election schedule for Poonch and Pallandri after reviewing the situation and “considering all relevant matters”. The commission clarified that the decision to postpone some of the polls was taken “only in the context of the current law and order situation to ensure that elections are held in a free, fair, transparent and peaceful environment”. The Election Commission’s decision comes in the wake of clashes that took place between protesters and law enforcement personnel in Poonch district’s Rawalakot on July 27, which reportedly resulted in several casualties. Rawalakot has been gripped by unrest since early June , with the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) staging sit-ins periodically. The JAAC, which has been demanding the abolishment of 12 seats in the local legislature reserved for refugees from Indian-held Kashmir, has been holding protests in the region for several weeks now. The government has accused militant elements “pursuing a foreign agenda and backed by Indian funding” of fomenting the unrest. Earlier this week, AJK Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal noted that the “law and order situation and the demands of the safety of voters play an important role in holding elections”. Responding to a question, he had said that under the AJK constitution, the current Legislative Assembly ceases to exist after August 4. “Even if elections cannot be held in two or a few more constituencies, one cannot say that the house is not complete or those who have returned cannot take oath or perform their functions,” he explained. He said the new assembly would still take oath after the completion of the August 10 polls. Election Commission addresses malpractice allegations On Friday, the Election Commission also responded to allegations of electoral malpractices and rigging, noting that a candidate claimed the previous day that Forms-24 had not been provided to polling agents at some polling stations. The allegation was made by PPP’s Raja Muhammad Shakeel Khan, which the Election Commission denied. “The Election Commission has not received any complaint regarding any constituency or polling station till now. The relevant presiding officers provided Forms-24 to polling agents at polling stations in line with law and the electoral practice,” its press release said. The Election Commission further said some candidates had also tried to create an impression that it allotted election symbols at a matter of its prerogative. “This impression is baseless and contrary to the facts. The symbols are allotted in accordance with the legal process described under AJK Elections Rules, 2020 and Form-42,” it said, adding that the commission allotted symbols without any bias towards or against any candidate. PML-N has already won: Rana Sana Meanwhile, PML-N leader and Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah addressed a public gathering in AJK’s Haveli, where he said his party had already won the required number of seats in AJK and was set to form the government. He said 23 seats were required for a simple majority in the assembly, while the PML-N had already won 24. Sanaullah told the rally’s participants that the PML-N would focus on development in AJK, which he said had been witnessed in the past every time the party was in the government in the Centre and AJK at the same time.

Domestic, foreign investors show interest in Fesco privatisation: privatisation commission. ISLAMABAD: The Privatisation Commission (PC) on Friday said it had received a strong response from domestic and international investors for the privatisation of Faisalabad Electric Supply Company (Fesco). The commission said it had received 12 expressions of interest (EOIs) from prospective investors seeking to acquire a 51pc to 100pc stake in Fesco along with management control. The EOIs were submitted by three Turkish investors, one Chinese investor and eight local investors. The three from Turkiye include Aktor Elektrik Enerji Yatırımları San. ve Tic. A.Ş., Genvera Enerji A.Ş. (Celik Group) and ⁠Cengiz Enerji Sanayii ve Ticaret A.Ş. The EOI from China came from Jiang Xi Electric Power Construction. The remaining eight Pakistani groups include Engro Energy Limited, Sapphire Fibers Limited, Hub Power Holdings, Lucky Cement, Shirazi Investments (Pvt) Limited (Atlas Group), Maple Leaf Cement and Kohinoor Textile, Nishat Mills Limited and Pak Elektron Ltd, and Artistic Milliners (Private) Limited and K-Electric Limited. The Privatisation Commission welcomed the interest shown by leading business groups in entering the power distribution sector and appreciated the investor community’s extensive engagement during domestic and international roadshows over the past six months. “This is an important milestone in the privatisation of Discos,” said Muhammad Ali, PC chairman and adviser to the prime minister on privatisation. “The strong response to Fesco reflects investor confidence in the potential of Pakistan’s electricity distribution sector and in the government’s commitment to a transparent, competitive and professionally managed process.” He further added that the commission “looks forward to engaging constructively with the prequalified investors through the due diligence process and discussing the contours of the post-privatisation regime”. The privatisation of Discos would “improve operational efficiency, modernise distribution infrastructure, strengthen customer service, reduce losses and support a more financially sustainable power sector”, the PC chairman said. “Over time, these measures will help create the conditions for more competitive electricity distribution and affordable, reliable power for consumers,” he added. In the next stage of the process, the EOIs and Statements of Qualification (SOQs) submitted by interested parties will undergo a comprehensive evaluation against the approved prequalification criteria. Applicants meeting the prescribed requirements will be invited to the next stage of the transaction, where they will be granted access to the Virtual Data Room (VDR) to conduct detailed buy-side due diligence. Fesco is among the three electricity distribution companies in Disco Batch-I privatisation , alongside Gujranwala Electric Power Company (GEPCO) and Islamabad Electric Supply Company (IESCO). The three are considered the most viable Discos among the 11 electricity distribution companies originally carved out of the Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda) in 1998. The deadlines for submission of EOIs for Gepco and Iesco are August 21 and September 7, 2026, respectively. PC said it would ensure an open, transparent and competitive privatisation process, undertaken in the public interest and in support of the federal government’s wider power-sector reform agenda.

Power consumers to pay 75 paisa per unit FCA in August bills. ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) on Friday notified an additional burden of Rs9.8 billion on electricity consumers for the August billing period due to a fuel cost adjustment (FCA) of 75 paisa per unit. The net average fuel cost in August would be around 41 paisa per unit higher than in July, when the FCA stood at Rs0.34 per unit. In its notification, Nepra said it had decided that the positive FCA for June 2026, amounting to Rs0.7503 per kWh, would apply to all consumer categories that opted for prepaid tariffs, except lifeline consumers, electric vehicle charging stations and prepaid electricity consumers. The adjustment applies to K-Electric (KE) as well as power distribution companies (Discos) that originated from Wapda. The regulator said the adjustment would also apply to consumers under the incremental consumption package. Discos and KE are required to reflect the fuel charges adjustment for June 2026 in the billing month of August 2026. The FCA is reviewed every month as per the tariff regime applicable across the country and is usually applicable to the consumer’s bills for one month only. The Central Power Purchasing Agency (CPPA) had reported that the actual average fuel charges component for June 2026 was Rs8.9138/kWh, compared with the reference fuel charges component of Rs7.7138/kWh approved in the applicable notified consumer-end tariff. Accordingly, it had demanded Rs1.20 per unit additional FCA for June 2026. After certain adjustments, Nepra worked out the actual fuel component of the tariff at Rs8.4641, thereby allowing a lower FCA of Rs0.75 per unit in August instead of Rs1.20. The power division and its entities had reported a 5.6 per cent decline in overall generation in June compared to the projected level. Nepra expressed concern over partial loading charges amounting to Rs4.9 billion. CPPA, however, argued that these charges were not due to operational inefficiencies but resulted from reduced daytime demand caused by rooftop solar generation. Power plants were operated at partial load during solar hours and ramped up later to meet the evening increase in grid demand. The power division warned that renewable power sources, such as wind and solar, may need to be curtailed in the future if daytime demand declines significantly in the coming years. Under the tariff mechanism, changes in fuel cost are passed on to consumers only on a monthly basis through the automatic mechanism. On the other hand, quarterly tariff adjustments — based on variation in power purchase price, capacity charges, variable operation and maintenance costs, use of system charges and impact of transmission and distribution losses — are built in the base tariff by the federal government. Last week, the government indicated that it was working on another power tariff package as it sought about Rs1.20 per unit additional fuel cost from consumers to collect Rs15.7 billion in August for electricity consumed in June.

SCBA backs call for new provinces, calls it 'step forward' for better governance. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) — a premier lawyers’ body — on Friday voiced support for the controversial proposal recently put forward by Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Naqvi regarding the creation of new provinces in the country. Recently, while addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026, the interior minister had urged all political parties to resolve various national issues, including the question of creating new provinces. He termed this the only solution to improving the country’s overall condition, which he said had “collapsed”. Speaking at the Full Court Reference held at the Supreme Court (SC) in honour of Justice Musarrat Hilali on the occasion of her laying down her judicial robes, SCBA President Haroonur Rashid said the association endorsed and supported the suggestion to create new provinces. Headed by Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi, the reference was attended by SC judges both in person and via video link. The reference was also attended by Additional Attorney General (AAG) Chaudhry Aamir Rehman, representatives of the SCBA and the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC), senior members of the legal fraternity, court officers, media representatives and others. “The association believes that any constitutional measure for the creation of more provinces would be a step forward towards an enhanced governance system through devolved and equitable administration at the grassroots level, the creation of equal opportunities for parallel economic development, and stronger political stability in the country,” the SCBA president said. He added that the creation of more provinces would also improve the standard of living by addressing the economic challenges faced by the people of the country. Meanwhile, in its 250th meeting held in Islamabad on Friday, the PBC — the apex body of the legal fraternity — said it firmly believed that all constitutional matters must be addressed strictly within the framework of the Constitution. The PBC deliberated upon the issue of the creation of new administrative units and provinces in the country. It reaffirmed through a resolution that the legal fraternity was committed to upholding the Constitution, and that members were of the unanimous view that the question of creating new provinces should be considered in accordance with the constitutional principles and procedures. The resolution emphasised that all political parties, irrespective of their political differences, should act in the “larger national interest” and initiate a “comprehensive and meaningful dialogue” for the betterment of the country and its people. The PBC resolved that, if the establishment of new provinces was deemed necessary, it must be carried out strictly in accordance with the Constitution through due parliamentary process and national consensus. The PBC also authorised its Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti and the chairman of its Executive Committee to organise a national seminar by inviting leaders of all political parties represented in Parliament, as well as representatives of provincial bar councils, for meaningful dialogue and to develop a broad-based national consensus. The seminar would aim to strengthen the federation, promote good governance, ensure equitable administrative and economic development, and improve the welfare of the common man. On the other hand, the SCBA president said the association would continue supporting the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments . He said the association believed that the amendments were an “important step towards ensuring parliamentary sovereignty, enhancing the separation of powers, and realising the concept that the judiciary should focus more on its fundamental constitutional responsibility of prompt dispensation of justice”. He also requested President Asif Ali Zardari to immediately give his assent to the recent appointment and confirmation of the high court judges recommended by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP) during its meeting on July 20 and 21. “SCBA believes that the appointment procedure adopted through the recent amendments were more balanced, comprehensive and transparent, since both the members of the judiciary and the Parliament were part of such a judicial process,” he said. Rashid also expressed his trust and confidence in the performance of the JCP, saying that its recent decisions regarding the appointment of judges to the high courts were based on merit, as “competent individuals” had been recommended for the highest judicial offices. Therefore, pendency in the grant of assent by the president may result in harming the Constitution as well as the interests of the country, he said. During the reference, the AAG, SCBA president and PBC vice chairman paid rich tributes to Justice Hilali’s professional integrity, judicial acumen and unwavering commitment to the administration of justice. They acknowledged the respect and admiration she earned across the bench and the bar through her principled conduct, independence and distinguished service, and conveyed their heartfelt best wishes for the next chapter of her life. In his address, CJP Afridi paid tribute to Justice Hilali, describing her judicial journey as one defined by “courage, perseverance and an unwavering commitment to justice”. He observed that her career was remarkable not only for the high judicial offices she held, but also for the barriers she broke and the enduring example she set for generations of lawyers, particularly women aspiring to leadership roles within the legal profession. “Justice Hilali’s career stands as a beacon of the growing participation and leadership of women in Pakistan’s justice sector,” Afridi said. Her professional journey, he noted, demonstrated that integrity, dedication and professional excellence remained the “true hallmarks of judicial leadership” and could inspire future generations of women to pursue careers of distinction in law and justice. The CJP also acknowledged Justice Hilali’s valuable contributions to strengthening the principles of judicial responsibility, institutional integrity, and public service throughout her tenure. PBC condemns NCCIA’s detaining of Islamabad-based journalists The PBC, in its Friday meeting, also strongly condemned the actions of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) in issuing notices to and detaining Islamabad-based journalists under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca). The council demanded that the government should immediately withdraw all such illegal notices and refrain from any actions that undermine the constitutional guarantees of freedom of expression and freedom of the press. “The legal fraternity has always stood in support of an independent and free media as a fundamental pillar of democracy and the rule of law, and will continue to oppose any attempt to intimidate, harass, or curtail the independence of the media,” it said.

Italy defies Spanish demand to lift border curbs over Ceuta migrant crisis. Spain threatened on Friday to impose restrictions on travellers from Italy unless Rome lifts by Sunday the border controls it introduced last week following a mass influx of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Italy swiftly responded, saying it would not accept “ultimatums or impositions” from Madrid, adding that it would keep in place its suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s conservative government had previously said the more robust travel checks would remain in force until the end of the month. The Spanish government said Italy’s decision to reintroduce controls on arrivals from Spain was “unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against the Spanish population”. It promised to adopt “proportionate measures” against Italy unless Meloni rolled back the new constraints by Sunday. However, in a toughly worded statement, Meloni’s office said Spanish authorities had themselves warned of a new migrant influx into Ceuta on August 15. It said it would only reconsider its decision once it was certain there was no new migration wave, no security or terrorism risk to Italy and no irregular migrants heading towards European territory. Spain’s Civil Guard has said it is aware of calls online for a fresh border crossing attempt at Ceuta on August 15, however it is not clear how many people might take part. Spain accuses Italy of ignoring facts As many as 72,000 people rushed to cross the border last week and dozens died in the attempt. Most have since returned to neighbouring Morocco but hundreds of unaccompanied minors remain in Ceuta. Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, justified its decision to partially suspend the EU’s border-free Schengen arrangements to prevent any of the migrants who entered Ceuta from travelling to Italy. There has been no indication that any of them want to travel to Italy, or have the money to pay for an airline ticket. Madrid said the Italian move was based on “spurious arguments” that lacked any factual basis because the migrants who entered Ceuta irregularly could not gain access to the Schengen area. Italy and Spain split on migration policy The dispute between the two EU allies marks a new low in relations between the right-winger Meloni, and Spain’s Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez. Meloni has positioned herself as one of Europe’s leading advocates of tighter immigration controls, while Sanchez has generally defended a more liberal approach and recently backed a large-scale regularisation programme for undocumented migrants. “I think what were saying is reasonable. What doesn’t hold water at all is Italy’s stance towards Spain. The impression is that Ms Meloni is on a crusade,” Spain’s Youth Minister Sira Rego told Spanish public broadcaster TVE1 . In Friday’s statement, the Spanish government said Italy had registered the highest number of “irregular crossings in recent years”, with figures that have been double those of Spain.

JI protests cause traffic disruptions across Karachi. Several major thoroughfares in Karachi were blocked or affected by traffic disruptions on Friday as Jamaat-i-Islami held protest sit-ins in the city as part of a nationwide demonstration against the petroleum levy. A day earlier, the party announced that it would stage sit-ins at 510 locations across the country by blocking major roads. In a traffic advisory issued, the Karachi traffic police warned that traffic flow could be affected due to the protests and sit-ins, with slow-moving traffic, temporary diversions and partial road closures expected on several major thoroughfares. The affected areas included Mazar-i-Quaid, Numaish Chowrangi, Saddar, Sharea Faisal, Sharae Pakistan, UP Mor, Power House Chowrangi, Defence Housing Authority, Sea View, Shahrah-i-Orangi, Hub River Road, Super Highway and National Highway. The traffic police advised citizens to avoid travelling to the affected areas unless necessary, and urged them to select alternative routes and allow extra travel time before setting out. Meanwhile, according to the latest updates shared on JI Karachi’s official X account, party workers had begun staging sit-ins at the announced locations. According to the updates, workers had blocked the road leading to Natha Khan from Sharea Faisal. The Super Highway and Hub River Road were also blocked. Moreover, the road leading from Sharea Faisal Nursery Bus Stop to Airport had also been blocked. ‘Fuel for political point-scoring’ Responding to the protest, Sindh government spokesperson Sadia Javed said the petroleum levy was a federal matter and questioned why Karachi’s citizens were being “punished” through road closures. “Jamaat-i-Islami is using the protest to score political points instead of serving the public,” she alleged, adding that the party should focus on the performance of its local government representatives to improve conditions for Karachi’s residents. She said it was unacceptable for a few hundred protesters to hold a city of millions hostage by disrupting traffic and daily life, adding that such politics should come to an end. “Blocking roads does not serve the public; instead, it adds to their difficulties,” Javed said, questioning how ambulances and patients could reach hospitals when major roads were closed. “If Jamaat-i-Islami is sincere in its concerns, it should raise the matter at the relevant forums and in Parliament rather than resorting to protests that disrupt public life,” she said. Javed also warned that the party should not use Karachi’s residents as “fuel for political point-scoring” and stressed that authorities would not allow anyone to take the law into their own hands, block roads or damage public property under the guise of protest. Other parts of country Meanwhile, JI workers also gathered at the designated sit-in locations in other provincial capitals, including Lahore, Quetta, Peshawar and Islamabad. In Lahore, protesters blocked Qurtaba Chowk, where JI Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman addressed a sit-in. In Islamabad, a demonstration at Chungi No. 26 was addressed by JI Deputy Emir Liaqat Baloch, the party’s Islamabad chapter chief Nasrullah Randhawa, and traders’ representative Kashif Chaudhry. The party claimed some clashes broke out between police and protesters during the demonstration. In Sindh, protesters also staged sit-ins in Thatta, Matiari, Tando Allahyar, Shikarpur and other districts.

What is the Patriot missile system and why are supplies depleted worldwide?. First used in the 1991 Gulf War, the US Patriot air defence system has seen demand spike sharply this year, with supplies of interceptor missiles depleted by Ukraine’s war against the Russian invasion and the widening war in the Middle East. Ukraine is urgently seeking more Patriot interceptors to defend against a nightly barrage of Russian ballistic missile strikes. But the Iran war has drained arsenals in the US and the Gulf, and some European countries are holding onto missiles they may need for their own defence. The following are some details about the Patriot air defence system, one of the most advanced weapons in the US arsenal. What is the Patriot system? Patriot, short for Phased Array Tracking Radar for Intercept on Target, is a mobile surface-to-air missile defence system built by US weapons maker Raytheon Technologies that can be used in all kinds of weather and at long range. Developed in the 1980s, the Patriot system has been modernised over the past decades, expanding its capabilities and reach. It is slated to remain in service through 2048. A typical battery includes radar and control systems, a power unit, launchers, and support vehicles. The system can intercept aircraft, tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, depending on the interceptor used. What can the Patriot system do? The system has different capabilities depending on the type of interceptor used. The earlier PAC-2 interceptor uses a blast-fragmentation warhead that detonates in the vicinity of a target, while the PAC-3 family of missiles uses more accurate “hit-to-kill” technology to physically collide with the target. Raytheon makes the PAC-2 GEM-T interceptor, which can defeat smaller, short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or enemy aircraft. Lockheed Martin, the world’s largest arms maker, builds the more advanced PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE), which can hit longer-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, aircraft and also hypersonics. In July, Lockheed introduced a new interceptor, the PAC-3 Adapted Capability Effector (ACE), which it says will cost half as much while still being able to target short-range ballistic missiles, aircraft and cruise missiles. The system’s radar has a range of over 150 kilometres and can simultaneously track up to 100 potential targets, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) said in 2015. Although not originally designed to intercept hypersonic weapons, in May 2023 the US confirmed Ukraine had used the Patriot system to shoot down a Russian Kinzhal missile, which Moscow claims is hypersonic. Countries closely guard details about the number of targets destroyed by Patriot systems, although Ukraine said in January it had destroyed 250 targets, including 140 ballistic missiles. Patriot has also destroyed dozens of Iranian ballistic missiles in the Gulf, although details have not been released. How widely is it used? Raytheon has built and delivered over 240 Patriot fire units, according to its website. Raytheon and Lockheed together have manufactured thousands of interceptor missiles. Nineteen countries now operate the Patriot system, according to Raytheon, including the US, Germany, Poland, Ukraine, Japan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Egypt. Of these countries, 16 have the newest PAC-3 MSE missiles, while six to eight countries have requested additional missiles to replenish their depleted stocks. In this US Army handout photo released on June 1, 2026, a US Army air defence artilleryman conducts maintenance on an MIM-104 Patriot missile system, the army’s primary terminal-phase anti-ballistic missile system, at an undisclosed location in the Middle East. — AFP/File How much does it cost? A newly produced single Patriot battery costs over $1 billion, including $400 million for the system and $690m for the missiles in a battery, according to the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). Patriot PAC-3 interceptors are estimated at around $4m to $5m per missile. Why are supplies dwindling? Specific inventory numbers are classified, but CSIS estimates that about 65 per cent of US Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with less than 850 left on hand, down from 2,330 before the Iran war began. Current inventories in the Gulf states are also severely depleted, and several European countries have transferred some of their supplies to Ukraine , experts say. Saudi Arabia used about 86pc of its 2,800 PAC-3 interceptors in the first 38 days of combat, leaving it with 400 missiles left in April. Other Gulf nations used up similar amounts of their inventories, CSIS said. Are countries buying more Patriots to boost inventories? The US has approved the sale of 5,250 interceptors to Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates for replenishment. The US is also pressing ahead with talks on allowing Ukraine to make Patriot interceptor missiles, even after President Donald Trump cast doubt on such a deal, sources familiar with the discussions said. The talks include an option for Ukraine to build some components for final assembly elsewhere in Europe. Last month, the US Army awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6bn to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

Goods transporters to go on strike from Saturday after talks with govt fail. Goods transporters and oil tanker operators began suspending their services on Friday night after negotiations with the government failed, ahead of their nationwide wheel-jam strike scheduled for Saturday. All Pakistan Goods Transport Itehad spokesman and All Pakistan Goods Transport Owners Association President Mohammad Owais Chaudhry Advocate told Dawn that talks with Federal Minister for Communications Aleem Khan and other government officials had failed. He said the negotiations ended without a breakthrough, prompting transporters, including edible oil tanker operators, petroleum oil tanker operators, truckers, trailer operators and other intercity transporters, to proceed with their previously announced strike. “We have informed the government side about the problems we are facing and our concerns,” Chaudhry said, adding that the strike would continue until their demands were accepted. However, the minister has assured the transporters that he would discuss their demands, and the next round of talks would be held on Monday morning. The unified body of transporters had already announced that it would begin its wheel-jam strike from August 8, and warned that it would not be a token strike but an indefinite one. “Commercial goods carriers across the country have already been taken off the roads and will remain stationed at designated places during the protest period,” Chaudhry said. Among the key demands of the transporters is the uniform enforcement of axle-load limits across the country and permission for 10-wheel vehicles to carry up to 35 tonnes. They have also demanded reductions in diesel prices and toll taxes, besides seeking relief in withholding tax to ease the financial burden on the transport sector. The transporters have also called for the withdrawal of customs provisions that, according to the association, allow authorities to confiscate vehicles carrying goods found to be in violation of customs laws. Other demands include the withdrawal of the Punjab Highway Patrol’s powers to issue challans to commercial vehicles, an end to what the association described as unnecessary challans and excessive fines on motorways and highways, and measures to facilitate the issuance of heavy transport vehicle licences to drivers.

Efforts underway to end deadlock over judges’ appointments. • Govt’s legal team set to meet Presidency officials as summary remains pending with Zardari • Officials say matter now sub judice after petition filed in IHC ISLAMABAD: In a last-ditch effort to break the deadlock over judicial appointments, the government’s legal team has scheduled a meeting with its counterparts at the Presidency on Sunday, as authorities explore the possibility of unilaterally notifying the confirmation and appointment of high court judges. The development comes as the Islamabad High Court (IHC) has yet to issue its ruling on the maintainability of a petition challenging President Asif Ali Zardari’s alleged failure to assent to the recommendations of the Judicial Commission of Pakistan. The JCP, during its meetings on July 20 and 21, recommended the confirmation of four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court, a six-month extension for an additional judge of the Sindh High Court, and the appointment of 19 additional judges to the Lahore, Islamabad, Sindh and Balochistan high courts. Under Clause 8 of Article 175-A of the Cons­titution, the recommendations were forwarded to the prime minister, who then sent the summary to the president. However, the summary has remained pending with the president since then. Amid the stalemate, the government is examining the possibility of invoking Article 48(1) of the Constitution to issue the notifications through the law ministry, arguing that the president was required to act on the summary within a fortnight of its submission — a period that has since expired. However, government functionaries have maintained that with the matter now sub judice, notifications cannot be issued at this stage. Sources said the government’s legal team planned to pursue an “out-of-court” settlement with its counterparts at the Presidency. The president’s legal team has raised certain objections to the JCP proceedings, noting that nearly all nominees proposed by the PPP were rejected. They also conveyed that some candidates recommended for appointment have criminal records. The Presidency’s legal team contends that Article 175-A does not prescribe a specific timeframe for the president’s action and that the provision cannot be overridden by Article 48(1) to bypass the Presidency. They have also referred to Article 48(2), which empowers the president “to act in his discretion in respect of any matter in respect of which he is empowered by the Constitution to do so” and states that validity of anything done by the president shall not be called into question on any ground whatsoever. Sources in the Presidency cautioned that any unilateral action in such a sensitive matter would be a “political and legal disaster”. According to them, the only way forward is to reach a consensus through democratic means. They warned that bypassing the prescribed procedure could trigger significant complications and suggested that any ambiguity regarding Articles 48(1), 48(2) and 175-A(8) should be resolved through mutual consultation between the president and the prime minister rather than through unilateral action. On the other hand, government sources maintained that judicial appointments were governed by constitutional provisions and that any deadlock must be resolved strictly in accordance with the Constitution. Meanwhile, the IHC has reserved its verdict on the maintainability of a petition filed by advocate Luqman Chaudhary through his counsel Zahid Chaudhry, seeking a direction to the president to approve the summary. During Thursday’s hearing, Justice Arbab Muh­ammad Tahir questioned how the court could issue directions to the president and reserved his order. It was initially expected that the ruling would be issued the same day, but Justice Arbab left his office without delivering it. The order was then anticipated on Friday morning, but the file had not been returned from the judge’s chamber by the close of business. The delay has already created practical complications. Four additional judges of the PHC, whose confirmations were recommended by the JCP, ceased to hold office after their tenure expired on Aug 4 due to the absence of formal notifications. Similarly, an additional judge of the SHC, whose term was extended by six months, relinquished office after his tenure expired on July 29. Minister of State for Law and Justice Barrister Aqeel Malik said the government would resolve the matter within the constitutional framework and in accordance with the principles laid down by the superior courts. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs327.62 per litre while HSD will cost Rs380.86 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on HSD. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will apply from August 8 to 10. The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

KP amends controversial law on lawmakers’ privileges. • Provisions for lifetime blue passport scrapped; number of lifetime arms licences for MPAs reduced to four • Assembly resolves to resist ‘proposed takeover’ of Hazara areas by federal government PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Assembly on Friday withdrew controversial provisions from the recently enacted KP Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Act, 2026 , including the issuance of official passports to lawmakers and their spouses for life. The provincial assembly had earlier in April passed the KP Provincial Assembly (Powers, Imm­unities and Privileges) Act, 2026, granting blue passports to members and their spouses, arms licences, blanket immunity from preventive detention, and making the speaker’s permission mandatory before arresting members on criminal charges. However, the law faced harsh criticism from the media and the general public, prompting KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi to order a review of the legislation last week. KP Information Minister Shafi Jan also announced that the government would withdraw the controversial clauses and restore the law in accordance with the 1988 Act. According to the amendment tabled by treasury lawmaker Ghazi Ikram during a sitting chaired by KP Assembly Speaker Baber Saleem Swati, the house passed the KP Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Amendment Act, 2026. The controversial provisions were withdrawn, and official passports will now remain valid only for the parliamentary tenure of lawmakers, in accordance with federal law. Also, the number of lifetime non-prohibited bore arms licences was also reduced from eight to four. The concerns raised by the journalist community over enhanced fines and punishments were also addressed, with both fines and punishments being reduced. Territorial integrity The house also unanimously passed a resolution over the possible alteration of the territorial jurisdiction of KP by annexing some parts of the province to the federal territory. The resolution, moved by treasury lawmaker Akbar Ayub, stated that Haripur, Abbottabad and all other districts were integral parts of KP and could not be annexed to any other part of the country. It added that any changes — whether administrative, political, financial or aimed at controlling natural resources — would be against the law. It stated that the residents of the province had constitutional rights over KP’s minerals, forests, hydel projects and other natural resources, and that any direct or indirect attempt to take control of these resources was unacceptable. The resolution stated that any changes to the province’s geographical boundaries for personal interests or political objectives would violate the Constitution and could harm the federation. It strongly condemned any such plan and demanded that the federal government reject such suggestions and respect KP’s geographical, constitutional and administrative status. The resolution added that the provincial assembly, the elected government and the people of KP would take all democratic and peaceful steps to safeguard the province’s geographical sovereignty, constitutional rights, provincial autonomy and natural resources, and would never hesitate to make any sacrifice. The house appealed to all political parties, the legal fraternity, public representatives, civil society, youth and the media to make a joint effort to protect the province’s geographical boundaries and the constitutional rights of its residents. “This house warns the federal government to refrain from making any geographical changes, as such a step will never be acceptable to the people of KP and could harm inter-provincial harmony and national unity,” the resolution read, demanding that the federal government publicly reject any such proposal. Source of revenue During the sitting, MPA Fazal Ilahi said that annexing parts of KP was a conspiracy and was unacceptable, adding that the province generated significant revenue from those areas. Earlier, treasury MPA Sultan-e-Rom informed the house that militancy had returned to Swat district after several years of relative peace. He questioned how long the people would continue to tolerate bombings. He said militants began reappearing in 2022, but massive public protests against their presence helped restore relative normalcy. However, he added that explosions continued to occur across KP and recalled the bloodshed in Swat. “We would rather accept death than face displacement again,” he said. Prescriptions In her call-attention notice, opposition lawmaker Meher Sultana of the PPP informed the house that there was no law requiring doctors to prescribe medicines by their generic names rather than by brand names. She said handwritten prescriptions were often illegible, placing an unnecessary financial burden on patients. She urged the health department to enact legislation requiring doctors to prescribe medicines by their generic names instead of brand names. Health Minister Khal­eequr Rehman informed the house that the matter fell under the jurisdiction of the federal government because the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) registered medicines under brand names. He said there was currently no policy requiring prescriptions by generic name but acknowledged that the issue was open to debate. However, he also argued that prescribing generic names could give medical store owners greater discretion to dispense medicines of their own choice. Opposition lawmaker Shahida Waheed of the ANP informed the house that Mardan Medical Complex catered to patients from Mardan and several other districts, but its CT scan and MRI machines had remained out of order, causing immense hardship for patients. Mr Zaman said the issue had been highlighted on social media and that notice had been taken. He said the CT scan machine was now functional and that the MRI machine would also be made operational soon. The sitting was later adjourned until 2pm on Monday. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

Pakistan joins Saudi Arabia, Turkiye in ‘all for one’ pact. • MBS, Shehbaz, Erdogan sign Makkah Joint Defence Agreement to boost ‘collective deterrence against any aggression’ • PM hopes accord will serve as ‘shield of peace’; Erdogan says alliance is open to other friendly nations • Saudi minister insists new bloc no threat to ‘any country’ ISLAMABAD: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday signed a joint defence pact in the holy city of Makkah, which empowers member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, which seeks to strengthen the collective security of the three states, was signed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Saudi Crown Prince and PM Mohammad bin Salman, and Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Al-Safa Palace. The signing of the agreement was announced by three countries through a joint statement, which was published by Pakis­tan’s Foreign Office (FO) and Saudi Arabia’s official SPA press agency. It said the pact reflected the three countries’ “shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond, in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future”. “The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” It also “provides for the enha­ncement of all aspects of defence cooperation” among the three countries, the statement added. The agreement is “guided by the longstanding historical ties among the three states, based on the enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity that unite them, and building upon their shared strategic interests and longstanding defence cooperation”. During the Makkah Summit for Joint Defence, the “distinguished relations” between the three countries were reviewed, “along with a number of issues of mutual interest”, the statement noted. From Pakistan’s side, Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, and Defence Minister Khawaja Asif were also present at the signing ceremony. The defence and foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Turkiye were in attendance as well. Following the formal signing of the pact, photos released by Saudi media showed the world leaders offering prayers at the Al-Safa Palace, overlooking the Holy Ka’aba. ‘Shield of peace’ PM Shehbaz Sharif described the signing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement as a “historic pact”, saying the three countries were united by faith, friendship and a shared commitment to peace and security. In a post on X, the prime minister said he was honoured to sign the agreement alongside the Saudi crown prince and the Turkish president. He said the pact would serve as a “shield of peace” for generations and expressed hope that it would bring prosperity to the three countries and the wider Muslim world. Shehbaz also appreciated Field Marshal Asim Munir’s efforts and dedication towards the agreement. Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan said that the signing of the joint defence agreement by the crown prince, the president of Türkiye and the prime minister of Pakistan underscored the depth of the fraternal and strategic relations between the three countries. He said the agreement marked an important milestone in their defence cooperation and reflected their shared desire to coordinate efforts to address challenges and threats affecting regional security and stability. He added that the pact embodied the three countries’ shared political will to safeguard security, support a more secure regional environment and pave the way for greater development and prosperity. Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the agreement “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc”. “Nor is it linked to any nuclear ambitions or arms race; rather, it is focused on building sustainable capabilities,” he wrote on X. He noted that the deal “does not constitute a threat to the security of any country in the region, nor does it represent an escalation of tensions between any two states”. The Saudi official further said the agreement “does not supersede or replace any existing bilateral or multilateral agreements between these countries”. ‘Open to other nations’ Turkish President Erdogan also reiterated this sentiment, saying that the pact targets no country and remains open to participation of other friendly nations seeking peace, prosperity and stability in the region. In a post on the Turkish social platform NSosyal, Erdogan said on Friday the agreement, based on the principle of collective deterrence, would strengthen security and defence cooperation, joint defence industry projects and counterterrorism efforts. He said the agreement also reaffirms the right to self-defence as defined under Article 51 of the UN Charter. “The agreement does not target any country and is open to the participation of all brotherly countries seeking peace, prosperity and stability in our region,” Erdogan said. Türkiye, he added, would firmly maintain its principled stance in favour of resolving conflicts and crises through dialogue and diplomacy, based on respect for international law and in line with its vision of regional ownership.
