Watchdogs call for scrapping foreign press curbs. KARACHI: As concern grows over recent restrictions imposed on foreign media outlets operating in the country, global human rights watchdogs have termed the fresh guidelines issued by the government “an attack on press freedom”. Until the new government restrictions were first circulated widely over the weekend, only foreign citizens working as journalists were routinely subject to controls on movement outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. Now, Pakistani journalists, fixers and others working for foreign media will need government permission to travel and report outside those three major cities and must register with the government – even for leisure travel. The controls mark “an alarming step” in Pakistan’s “narrowing space for press freedom,” said Patricia Gossman of Human Rights Watch, calling for them to be “immediately reversed”. Meanwhile, Amnesty International said on Friday that the restrictions on foreign news outlets, extending to local staff of these organisations, under the new Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines, 2026 were “an attack on press freedom”. “Why is the government afraid of truth?,” the statement questioned. Earlier, the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) had called on authorities to withdraw what it termed “draconian new guidelines”. “The Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines open the door for Pakistani authorities to further restrict international media coverage, prevent journalists from reporting freely outside Pakistan’s three main cities, and risk exposing them to administrative retaliation,” CPJ Afghanistan and Pakistan Representative Waliullah Rahmani said in a statement. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, and the country’s main journalist union, the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists, have already condemned the ‘Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026’. According to CPJ, the five-page guidelines were introduced days after the government criticised international reporting on elections and protests in Azad Kashmir and accused Al Jazeera of engaging in “yellow journalism,” a term for sensational reporting. Subsequently, foreign media representatives were ordered out of Azad Kashmir earlier this week. The Financial Times , one of several outlets operating in Pakistan, told Reuters it “supports the ability of journalists to report freely and independently.” A spokesperson for Reuters said, “Journalists should be free to report the news wherever they are.” In a statement, the BBC also said it was “extremely concerned” about the new guidelines, and called on Pakistani authorities to reverse the “unnecessary restrictions”. “Freedom of the press is increasingly under pressure around the world and this unwelcome change in approach is a step backwards for Pakistan’s media freedom,” a spokesperson for the broadcaster said in a statement. According to New York Times , Pakistan ranks 153rd out of 180 countries in the Repo­rters Without Borders’ Press Freedom Index. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

Broad Peak search for bodies of 3 climbers paused. • Mission to resume once weather improves • Bodies of Nirmal Purja, four other foreign climbers flown to Islamabad for repatriation to their respective countries GILGIT: The search operation to recover the remains of Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi and two foreign climbers missing after the deadly Broad Peak avalanche has been suspended due to the continuing risk of fresh avalanches, rescue officials said on Friday. Search teams spent eight days trying to locate the rem­ains of Sohail Sakhi, American climber Sarah Mallory Geis, and Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa before deteriorating conditions forced authorities to halt the mission. Ayaz Shigri, General Secre­t­a­­ry of the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP), said a leg believed to belong to Geis had earlier been recovered. He added that Nawang Thindu Sherpa’s body has been located but cannot be retrieved because it lies in a highly dangerous, avalanche-prone area. He said rescue efforts would resume once weather conditions improve and the area is safe. ACP President Major Gen-eral (retd) Irfan Arshad Khan also confirmed the suspension, saying rescue teams would return to Broad Peak when conditions permit. Meanwhile, the bodies of five foreign climbers killed in the Bro­ad Peak avalanche were flown from Skardu to Islamabad on a private airline flight on Fri­day for repatriation. They were received by Airport Mana­ger Aftab Ali Shah Gillani, ASF Chief Security Officer Mu­­ham­mad Rashid, and other officials before being transfer­red to the mortuary at the Pims, where they will remain until repatriation arrangements are completed. The bodies had been airlifted from Broad Peak Base Camp to Skardu and temporarily kept at the CMH, Skardu. Mr Khan said the deceased climbers were wrap­ped in their national flags bef­o­­re being handed over to airport au­­thorities by the Pakistan Army. The remiains of three climbers will be repatriated to Nepal, while Purja’s body will be sent to the UK. Meanwhile, Chinese climber Zhong’s family is expected in Islamabad to collect his body. With input from Mohammad Asghar Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

NAB chief urges withdrawal of Rs500m graft probe limit. • Tells Senate panel bureau’s hands are tied under amended law to act against govt officials • Says private sector accounts for 45pc of corruption ISLAMABAD: The National Account­abi­lity Bureau (NAB) on Friday urged the government to withdraw a restriction that prevents it from taking action against government officials accused of corruption involving less than Rs500 million. “Untie our hands and withdraw the Rs500m restriction; otherwise, people [government officials] will become addicted to committing corruption,” NAB Chairman retired Lt Gen Nazir Ahmed said during a meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Law and Justice. Under the amended NAB law, the anti-graft watchdog cannot take up cases involving amounts below Rs500m. As a result, a large number of cases it had been pursuing were transferred to other departments, such as the Federal Investigation Agency. Mr Ahmed said that because of the restriction, a station house officer (SHO) of the police enjoyed more powers than a NAB investigation officer. A NAB prosecutor general read out the amended law governing the anti-graft body, saying the bureau could not take action against members of the federal or provincial cabinets or their committees. At this, committee chairman Senator Farooq Naek said that although NAB could not act against cabinet decisions or those of its committees, it could proceed against individuals who violated those decisions or engaged in corrupt practices. He said NAB had been established to investigate mega corruption cases, such as the Rs1.20 trillion Neelum-Jhelum Hydropower Project, on which Rs513bn had been spent. It had now emerged, he said, that the design prepared by the National Engineering Services Pakistan (Nespak) was faulty. “It is a joke played on the people of Pakistan. We all know that corruption was committed during the construction of roads,” he added. JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza, also a member of the committee, said the Rs500m threshold should also be withdrawn in cases involving politicians. The NAB chairman said the media usually highlighted cases involving politicians more vigorously than other corruption cases. However, he said politicians accounted for six per cent of the country’s overall corruption, while government officials were responsible for 11pc. ‘Private sector’ “We are always asked to pursue cases against politicians. However, the private sector, including the sugar mafia, accounts for more than 45pc of the country’s total corruption,” he added. The committee chairman asked why NAB did not take action against officials of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and the police. Mr Ahmed replied that the FBR did not fall within NAB’s jurisdiction. Senator Abdul Qadir urged NAB to investigate the petroleum sector, where wells had been drilled for oil and gas exploration over the past 20 years without any production. “If NAB takes action on this, millions of people could benefit from cheaper oil and gas,” he added. The committee also received a detailed briefing from NAB, during which its chairman claimed the bureau had recovered assets worth $64bn, including state and private land. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

Danger ahead. PAKISTAN has already paid a heavy human price this monsoon, even as another dangerous spell approaches. NDMA figures covering June 26 to Aug 7 record 151 deaths — 73 of them children — and 448 injuries, besides damage to more than 1,200 houses and dozens of bridges and kilometres of roads. Chitral shows how quickly such destruction multiplies into other emergencies. Glofs, cloudbursts and flash floods have washed away bridges and severed roads, leaving communities unable to reach healthcare. Attendance at Lower Chitral’s district headquarters hospital has fallen by around 55pc, while patients from some isolated villages have stopped arriving altogether. Doctors are already reporting gastroenteritis and dysentery and fear outbreaks of typhoid and malaria. Pregnant women unable to reach hospitals face particular danger, while post-traumatic stress is emerging among disaster-hit communities. The situation shows us how extreme weather kills not only through torrents and collapsing homes, but also by cutting people off from medicines, clean water and timely treatment. NDMA, Rescue 1122, district administrations and the National Highway Authority have been involved in evacuations, relief distribution and restoration work. But each disaster exposes the distance between issuing warnings and protecting people. Chitral residents have complained of slow road clearance, delaying access to villages where medical needs are mounting. Warning equipment in parts of KP has previously been damaged or stolen, pointing to weaknesses in maintenance and local ownership. District authorities must know which settlements require evacuation, where residents will be taken, how alerts will get to people without mobile connectivity and how food, medicines and medical teams will reach communities. Such plans must be prepared before an emergency, not improvised after valleys are cut off. Medical camps, safe-water points and emergency stocks should be positioned in vulnerable valleys. There is particular urgency now. PMD’s Aug 7 outlook warns of moderate to heavy rainfall over the upper catchments of all major rivers from Aug 10 to 13, including KP, GB, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad and upper Punjab, with river and tributary flows expected to rise. Authorities should use this window to pre-position heavy machinery, boats, temporary bridges, fuel, food, drinking water, medicines and mobile clinics. Pregnant women, elderly people and patients requiring regular treatment should be identified for early evacuation, while alternative communication systems must be ready where conventional networks may fail. Shelters should be accessible and evacuation routes communicated before conditions deteriorate. Pakistan cannot control the monsoon or the instability of its glaciers. But it can control how seriously it acts on warnings. With the warning already given, the task now is to ensure that the next spell does not deepen an already heavy human toll. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

The supreme sacrifice. THE police are a vital pillar of our social fabric, serving not only as guardians of the law but also as protectors of the community, said President Asif Ali Zardari on Police Martyrs Day on Aug 4. “Their exemplary courage, firm dedication and ultimate sacrifice in the service of the nation will always inspire pride and command the deepest respect of every citizen of Pakistan,” he added. The prime minister, too, honoured the bravery of police officers who had laid down their lives in the line of duty, noting that the force displays “exceptional professionalism and unflinching resolve” in the nation’s fight against terrorism, violent extremism and crime. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies reported that the first seven months of 2026 witnessed 2,786 deaths linked to terrorist violence and counterterrorism operations — 434 security forces’ personnel lost their lives, including 152 police officials in KP and 89 in Balochistan. So far, July has been the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security officials offering the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty, compared to 38 fatalities a month earlier in June. This is an unprecedented 195 per cent increase in the deaths of law enforcers. At least eight suicide attacks were recorded last month, the highest number in a single month during the past decade. The recent deadly attack near a police station in Swat caused 17 fatalities. As this paper rightly asserted after the Swat bombing, it “is far too high a toll, and the state needs to urgently refine its CT strategy to prevent further loss of precious lives”. Following Police Martyrs Day, one of us convened a forum of serving and retired police officers to discuss the current vulnerabilities and challenges faced by police in general, and those in KP and Balochistan in particular. The trajectory and tenor of violence in these provinces have distinct traits. KP has been on the receiving end since 9/11, paying a huge price in the so-called war against terror. Since Kabul’s takeover by the Taliban in August 2021, violence and bloodshed have assumed greater intensity. Acts of terror have risen exponentially, with fatalities among security forces and civilians progressively rising each year. The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel. The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel. Balochistan is facing its fifth (and longest) phase (20 years) of insurgency by separatists. Nawab Akbar Bugti’s killing in a cave near Kohlu in August 2006 was an unfortunate incident that led to a sharp escalation in Baloch militancy. The terrorist nexus of the BLA, BRA and BLF has added lethality to insurgent attacks. BLA’s Majeed Brigade is well-equipped and emulates TTP’s violent tactics. It has superior weaponry, indicating the role of hostile foreign agencies in fomenting unrest in the province. The police’s challenge has increased manifold now that the entire province has been converted into police jurisdiction. The gap in human resources, infrastructure and training for the job is pronounced. A recent significant development is the incursion of the TTP in the Pakhtun areas as witnessed in the tragic July 6 attack on the Mangi Dam pumping station police post by the terrorist group, leading to the kidnapping and killing of 27 policemen. Our deliberations have led to identification of certain vulnerabilities and constraints that beset the police operating in the terror and insurgency-prone areas of KP and Balochistan where violence is driven by a combination of enhanced militant capability, difficult terrain, cross-border dynamics and institutional challenges. The following issues are pertinent. Intelligence coordination and information sharing: Coordination between police, intel agencies and other law-enforcement institutions is not always seamless; delays in sharing actionable intelligence reduce the ability to prevent attacks or intercept terrorists before they strike. Inadequate protection of police personnel and infrastructure: Police stations, check posts and patrols are often targeted because they have limited physical protection, surveillance or early-warning capabilities; some units in dangerous zones lack sufficient protective equipment, secure transport and modern communication systems, increasing their vulnerability. Limited capacity and community-based policing: In remote and conflict-affected areas, a trust deficit exists between communities and police. Without strong local engagement, authorities receive fewer timely reports about suspicious activities, allowing terrorist networks to operate with greater freedom. The merger of Fata into KP and the conversion of ‘B’ areas into ‘A’ areas in Balochistan was undertaken without adequate planning, capacity building or the provision of necessary financial and operational resources. The denial of these essential resources has exposed both police and the civil armed forces to avoidable risks, contributing to a significant increase in casualties among personnel. Expressions of support and appreciation for their sacrifices must therefore be matched by meaningful investment in manpower, training, equipment, intelligence, mobility and welfare to enable police to perform their duties effectively and safely. As former police chiefs we acknowledge that the challenges faced by current police commanders are far more daunting and require a strategic and operational rethink to restore order and promote peace in the restive borderlands in Pakistan’s north and south. Serving and retired police officers agree that the revised CT NAP must be implemented through professional tactics and strategic oversight. Here are a few recommendations at the operational level. Strengthen intelligence-led policing: Establish integrated intelligence coordination mechanisms that facilitate timely information-sharing among police, intelligence services and local administration; expand analytical capabilities and use technology to identify emerging threats, while ensuring operations remain consistent with the law and human rights standards. Modernise police protection and training: Upgrade security at vulnerable police facilities through better surveillance, convoy drills, ambush response, communications and sound infrastructure; provide regular training in CT tactics, drone threat response, incident command and officer safety, along with appropriate protective equipment. Expand community policing and public partnerships: Build stronger relationships with local communities, tribal elders, religious leaders and CSOs to improve trust and encourage lawful reporting of suspicious activities; develop accessible mechanisms for citizens to share information confidentially; promote public awareness programmes that strengthen resilience. The trend of rising terrorist attacks against, and thus higher casualties among, the police must be immediately stopped before it derails the entire CT effort in KP and Balochistan. This requires a balanced approach that combines effective policing, better intelligence coordination, professional training and meaningful community engagement. Strengthening these areas can enhance the safety of police personnel while also increasing public confidence and contributing to a more secure environment for local communities. Finally, for the policymakers and political leadership, our message is simple: invest in police and trust them to deliver. The writers are former inspectors-general of police. Before AI hits the grid. PAKISTAN’S announcement that it would allocate 2,000 megawatts of electricity for Bitcoin mining and AI data centres has triggered a predictable debate: can the country afford to supply that much power? It is an important question, but not the most useful one. Bitcoin mining, AI training and real-time digital services do not exactly place identical demands on the electricity system. Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available. It is about when and where electricity is needed, whether the network can deliver it reliably, and how that demand is managed during periods of stress. During the hottest months, cooling demand pushes the grid towards its limits. At other times, generation capacity remains underused. But nationally available capacity does not automatically translate into reliable electricity at the location and hour a data centre requires it. Transmission constraints, substation capacity and power quality matter just as much as the headline allocation. The better question is this: how should this new demand be designed and integrated into the electricity system from the outset? Data centres are not ordinary consumers. Their location, cooling systems, computing equipment and grid connections are decided before construction begins. That gives Pakistan a rare opportunity to shape a major new category of demand before it becomes embedded in the system. But doing so requires recognising that not all computing demand is the same. Some services are highly sensitive to delay. User-facing AI applications, financial platforms and communications systems may require continuous availability. Their loads cannot simply be switched off whenever the grid comes under pressure. Other workloads may offer more flexibility. Certain forms of data processing and model training can be scheduled within broader time windows, distributed across locations or paused at planned checkpoints, depending on how the systems are designed. Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available. Where genuine flexibility exists, it can be reflected in tariffs and connection agreements. Eligible workloads could be scheduled outside critical peak hours. Operators could provide more accurate demand forecasts, limit abrupt changes in consumption, or use storage to reduce pressure on the network during short periods of stress. This is not a hypothetical mechanism. The UN referred to Ireland as a “cautionary tale” when the country faced a severe energy crisis because data centres consume roughly 23 per cent of the nation’s total electricity — nearly rivalling the power used by all residential homes combined. Ireland’s grid operator now assesses new data centre connections in constrained areas partly on whether the applicant can prove its demand is flexible, and writes that commitment directly into the connection agreement rather than leaving it voluntary. Pakistan can build the same discipline in from the start, instead of retrofitting it once the grid is already under strain, the way Ireland had to. Pakistan does not need to begin from scratch. The country already has a cloud-governance and accreditation framework. The Cloud Office is mandated to set standards and compliance requirements for cloud service providers, while the existing accreditation criteria cover security, service availability, resilient power infrastructure and recognised data centre certification. What the framework does not yet fully address is how efficiently these facilities use electricity and water, or how they interact with the wider power system. The Ministry of IT & Telecom’s own concept note identifies this gap. It notes that the current framework does not explicitly prescribe standards for energy management, environmental performance, power usage effectiveness, water usage effectiveness or renewable energy integration. It proposes a national sustainability framework for data centres to fill that gap. That is the right direction. But the framework should go one step further by connecting digital-infrastructure planning with power sector planning. Large facilities should provide credible forecasts of their electricity and water demand. Projects should be assessed against local network capacity, not simply national generation figures. Energy and water performance should be measured consistently. And tariffs should reward verified efficiency and flexibility rather than merely offering cheap electricity to large consumers. This is not anti-investment. Serious data centre investors already consider reliable power, cooling, environmental compliance and long-term energy security when choosing markets. Good standards are not a barrier to investment, but rather, a part of a credible investment proposition. The first generation of AI infrastructure will shape the one that follows. Early decisions on location, efficiency and grid connection will become precedents that are harder to change once major investments have been made. Pakistan does not need to wait for its grid to buckle before it asks this question, the way Ireland did. It has the chance to design demand before it hits the grid, not renegotiate it after the fact. The writer is director, Awareness and Outreach, National Energy Efficiency & Conservation Authority. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

Captain martyred, 7 terrorists killed in intelligence-based operation in Hangu: ISPR. The military media affairs wing said on Saturday that a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Hangu district. In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said security forces conducted an IBO in Hangu on Friday following reports about the presence of terrorists belonging to Fitna al Khawarij — a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. During the operation, troops effectively engaged the terrorists, it said. “In desperation, the khawarij took refuge inside a mosque, blatantly disregarding the sanctity of the place of worship. In ensuing fire exchange, seven khawarij , belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khawarij were sent to hell,” it said. The statement went on to say that during the exchange of fire, 27-year-old Captain Hamza Akram, a resident of Punjab’s Narowal district who was “leading his troops from front and relentlessly pursuing” the terrorists, embraced martyrdom. “Weapons and ammunition were also recovered from the killed khawarij , who remained actively involved in numerous terrorist activities against the security forces and law enforcement agencies as well as killing of innocent civilians,” it said. ISPR said that a sanitisation operation was being conducted to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored terrorists in the area. President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to the martyred captain saying, “The motherland pays its profound tribute to the great sacrifice of its brave son.” “The entire nation is indebted to the eternal sacrifices of these brave sons for the motherland,” the president added, offering prayers for the bereaved family. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the martyred captain and offered his condolences to the bereaved family. He said that the martyred officer had paid the ultimate sacrifice for the homeland and would remain alive in our hearts. A day earlier, ISPR said 10 terrorists were killed in two separate engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It said that in the first encounter, a group of terrorists attempted to attack security forces’ checkposts in Azam Warsak area in South Waziristan, which was effectively thwarted, resulting in the deaths of eight terrorists. “In another encounter that took place in Dir district, own troops successfully neutralised two more khawarij ,” it added. Terrorist commander killed in Bannu Separately, security forces killed a key terrorist commander, identified as Jamidullah, during an operation in Jani Khel area of KP’s Bannu district, a security official said. The official said that the terrorist commander was involved in terrorist activities and was considered a quadcopter expert. The official said that security forces conducted the operation in Jani Khel on the basis of intelligence reports, during which Jamidullah was targeted and killed. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , an Islamabad-based think tank, violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed.

Trump administration to invest $3 billion in minerals projects to boost US defence supply chains. The US government will invest $3 billion in critical minerals and battery projects as part of a push to increase domestic production and boost national security and industrial policy, US President Donald Trump said on Friday. “We’re reclaiming America’s rightful place as the minerals superpower of the world,” Trump told more than 200 mining executives, educators, investors and fellow politicians at a roundtable at the State Department aimed at supporting the industry, which he said had not received enough attention from Washington in recent years. He announced a slew of investments during his speech, including a $1.4bn conditional loan from the Defence Department’s Office of Strategic Capital for Sila Nanotechnologies, which makes lithium-ion battery parts. The OSC also extended a $400 million conditional loan to scandium miner Sunrise Energy Metals and a $150m conditional loan to magnet developer Niron Magnetics. The US Export-Import Bank will lend $58m to Westwater Resources, Global Advanced Metals and 5E Advanced Materials, which Reuters reported earlier on Friday. “Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA,” Trump said. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and National Security Council official David Copley attended the announcement. Weapons stockpiles drive mineral demand The White House needs critical minerals to replenish weapons stockpiles depleted during the Iran conflict and reduce US dependence on Chinese supply chains. Several executives came with gifts for Trump. Tom Albanese, chairman of deep-sea mining firm American Ocean Minerals, gave Trump a gold replica of a nodule that the company hopes to mine from the Pacific seabed. Trump last year said he may bypass the UN-backed International Seabed Authority and issue international seabed mining licenses. Jim Litinsky, CEO of rare earths firm MP Materials, which is financially supported by the Pentagon, gave Trump magnets that had been produced for General Motors in the company’s Texas plant. Other attendees included executives from Lithium Americas , which is building the largest US lithium mine, NioCorp, which is building a scandium mine to supply defence contractor Lockheed Martin, and Energy Fuels , which received a $725m OSC conditional loan in June. US forces have burned through large numbers of precision-guided missiles and air-defence interceptors during the five-month-old US- Iran war. Defence officials and lawmakers have warned that replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints. The Trump administration has disputed reports of significant shortages. Supplies of minerals including rare earths, tungsten, germanium and scandium are essential for manufacturing precision-guided missiles, fighter aircraft, armored vehicles, infrared sensors and other advanced weapons systems, according to Pentagon officials and defence companies. Mining schools receive funding boost The Department of Energy on Friday hosted representatives from all 14 accredited US mining schools to promote mining careers and encourage more students to enter the field. The department announced $100m in grants to help boost educational programs and set a goal of doubling the number of mining-related graduates at the nation’s universities within two years. “We need to work on some systemic changes to how we as a nation want to offer our brightest students an opportunity to participate in this industry,” said Assistant Energy Secretary Audrey Robertson. The Pentagon also said it would fund $80m in projects at three US mining schools. Officials have pointed to China’s extensive network of mining universities as a key advantage in its dominance of global mineral production. Since returning to office, Trump has launched a $12bn strategic minerals stockpile , backed equity investments in companies developing US mines and processing facilities, and sought to limit defence contractors’ reliance on supplies from China. The administration says government support is needed to counter decades of Chinese investment that left Beijing dominant in the mining and processing of many strategic minerals. Australia’s government on Saturday welcomed the Trump administration’s loan to Sunrise Energy Metals, which is developing a scandium mine in the country’s New South Wales state. “The Sunrise Scandium Project hosts the world’s largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications,” Resources Minister Madeleine King said in a statement.

Explainer: Why jobseekers are protesting results of a major civil service exam. Young people applying for entry-level jobs in Sindh’s bureaucracy have been protesting that only 70 out of over 4,300 of them have passed the exam held by the Sindh Public Service Commission. They sat ten written papers for the Combined Competitive Examination (CCE), whose shockingly slim number of successful candidates was announced on May 6. This is how assistant commissioners, assistant directors and section officers at Grades 16 and 17 are hired. Lower than 16 is for drivers and clerks hired in the districts. The highest grade is 22. Think chief secretary level. The SPSC typically passes at least five candidates per seat in its written examinations. However, according to spokesperson Hifzullah Kaka, that doesn’t necessarily apply to the CCE. Nevertheless, the 2024 results still struck protesters as impossible to accept. Alarm bells started ringing when the detailed marks certificates were uploaded after the results were announced. For instance, the 100-mark optional subject Criminology with a single exam paper was shown as two papers worth 200 marks in the detailed marks certificates. “At first, we thought it might be a mistake,” said Farman Ali, a candidate leading the campaign. “But it wasn’t limited to Criminology. We saw the same issue in Environmental Science as well.” SPSC spokesperson Kaka did not respond to a request for clarification and declined to comment, saying that the matter was in court. When Dawn visited the SPSC on August 5, guards did not permit entry. By May 7, the day after results were uploaded, social media was flooded with allegations of manipulation to pass a favoured few. That’s when the Sindh Students Action Committee got organised, according to one of the protestors, Wajahat Ahmed. A rally was held after which the protestors decided to keep up the pressure by refusing to move from outside the SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. Protesters camp outside SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. The backlash prompted the SPSC to lean on anti-terrorism laws. Among those it acted against was a US-based journalist and YouTuber, Imtiaz Chandio, who, along with two social media activists, Fayyaz Hussain Shar and Rafiullah Qureshi, was booked in a terrorism case for spreading “false propaganda and inciting” the candidates. SPSC Assistant Secretary Muhammad Mustafa registered an FIR at the GOR police station citing multiple sections of the Pakistan Penal Code, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act. On May 13, a rally drew students from across Sindh, who marched from Hyderabad’s Daudpota Library to Thandi Sarak. The next day, MQM-P lawmaker Maaz Mahboob submitted a resolution in the Sindh Assembly against the results, expressing “grave concern over the alleged irregularities, violations of merit and lack of transparency.” The resolution demanded that the disputed results be suspended immediately and an independent forensic audit of the examination process, marking system, and merit list be conducted by the Punjab Forensic Lab or any other impartial institution. On May 14, protesters launched the Movement for Restoration of Meritocracy, a broader campaign against what they describe as nepotism and the erosion of merit in public recruitment. Its name appears inspired by and rhymes with the famous Movement for the Restoration of Democracy, or MRD, launched in the 1980s to challenge the military regime. Its slogan claps back at the SPSC’s press release telling future candidates to sit the upcoming examinations with “zeal and zest”. So the MRM banners say, ‘Restore meritocracy with zeal and zest’, according to Farman Ali. He works as a grade 11 clerk at the Federal Board of Revenue. “Being a government employee, it is difficult to execute protests and raise a voice,” he said. “Since the intensity of injustice was high, I risked all that.” Banners and posters put up by protesting candidates outside the SPSC head office in Hyderabad. Landing in court The protests swelled, and students filed petitions challenging the results. A few days later, the Sindh High Court suspended them and summoned SPSC officials with the complete examination record. It said everything would be on hold. “According to the interim order, further appointments and proceedings based on the [CCE-24] results were halted,” Advocate Kamran Ali Isran, one of the lawyers representing the candidates, told Dawn . On May 22, the court extended the suspension till June 9 as the SPSC said that the record had been sealed in compliance with the court order. The court wanted the SPSC to explain how it addressed complaints that it was not being transparent. A month later, the court told a district and sessions judge to collect the examination record of the candidates who had failed CCE-24, seal it on the spot and bring it to the next hearing. In response, the SPSC went to the newly created Federal Constitutional Court to challenge the Sindh High Court’s orders through its lawyer Advocate Hafiz Ahsaan Ahmad Khokhar. It argued that the exam was held transparently, fairly and in line with the laws that applied: the Sindh Public Service Commission Act, 2022, and the Recruitment Management Regulations, 2023. By July 16, the federal court suspended the Sindh High Court’s interim orders for an inquiry, a stop to interviews of successful candidates and a recheck for failed candidates. With those orders lifted, the SPSC went ahead with interviewing the 70 successful candidates. As the hearings continue, so do the protests, which have spread to Nawabshah, Ghotki, Qambar, Umerkot, Islamkot, and Gambat. “In Sindh, wherever you go, knock on any door and ask, you will find someone who has been a victim of the SPSC,” says Zabiullah Mastoi, one of the participants in Hyderabad. SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. According to journalist Imdad Soomro, who has covered SPSC for over a decade, the commission has long been a source of concern. “When I investigated it, I found that around 40 per cent of appointments were political, 40pc were made based on money, and only 20pc were on merit,” he claimed. “Gradually, merit came down to around 5pc, while the rest were political appointments or based on money.” Candidates who perform exceptionally well in the written examination are often eliminated at the interview stage, while those with lower written scores are given higher marks in the viva. The protesters say the court proceedings have done little to help. The camp continues, with candidates insisting they will stay until their demands are met: scrap the CCE-2024 and hold fresh exams, the chairman Muhammad Rizwan along with all commission members should resign, and an independent judicial commission should investigate SPSC examinations and recruitments for grades 16 and 17 over the past five years, among others. Govt restores original medical board for exhumation of Mir Raza’s body. • Corpse of IBA graduate to be dug up for fresh autopsy today • Exhumation planned for Friday postponed after family objected to abrupt reconstitution of board KARACHI: After a day of uncertainty over the exhumation of the body of IBA graduate and businessman Mir Raza Ali, the Sindh government on Friday evening restored the original medical board, which is set to exhume the body on Saturday (today). The exhumation, which was scheduled for Friday morning, was postponed after Raza’s family objected to the abrupt reconstitution of a medical board and inclusion of members from outside Karachi division. Raza’s body was found in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he went missing on July 28. On Thursday, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Raza’s father, Mir Hussain Ali, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed as the convener. Prof Dr Naseem Ahmed of Dow University of Health Sciences, Dr Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Amir Hassan Khan of Citizens Police Liaison Committee, Additional Police Surgeon Dr Sirichand, Dr Kamran Khan and Dr Daniyal Mirza of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre and Dr Mohammed Yaseen, the admin in-charge of the police surgeon office, were the other members of the board. However, in the small hours of Friday morning, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed to Prof Dr Zakiuddin from DUHS, Prof Dr Kazi Akbar and Prof Dr Abid Hussain Chang from Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences and Hyderabad Police Surgeon Dr Waseem Khan. On Friday morning, Raza’s family was present at the Tariq Road graveyard for the exhumation. But, the exhumation was deferred, with the counsel for Raza’s family, Jibran Nasir, telling the media that they had informed the investigating officer that the family had rejected the reconstituted board and would not accept an exhumation by it “under any circumstances”. Standing alongside Raza’s father, Advocate Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts and held the police, health department and the Sindh government responsible for the delay. The family could not allow the exhumation to be performed by members whose “qualifications and intentions were under question”, he added. He recalled that the previous night, DG-health dismissed the original board and reconstituted it, adding four names from Hyderabad. He claimed that following outcry over the reconstituted board, the DG-health then issued a “backdated notification at around 10am on Friday, stating that more members may be added, but the four chosen by him should also remain a part of it”. He added that they still had not been informed why the original board was reconstituted. The lawyer said they would not be making any demands to the police. Raza’s father was now directly raising questions to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, he said. He asserted that they only trusted the original eight-member board, adding, “Sindh government, they were hired by you. And if they are not competent enough, then how were they appointed in the first place?” Advocate Nasir also submitted a letter to the police surgeon on Friday, wherein he formally informed her of the family’s non-consent and stated that the reconstituted board was in “complete violation and negation” of the court’s order and had no legal basis. He held that it carried no binding value and was nothing “but a malicious attempt to interfere with judicial proceedings initiated by the court” and any directive in support of the board shall be viewed as a “further malicious attempt to provide cover to an illegal act and sabotage fair and transparent investigation”. He said the family had not consented to the exhumation by the reconstituted board and warned that any attempt to proceed with the exhumation under the reconstituted medical board will be a violation of the dignity of the deceased, will put evidence at risk and will be a “blatant” contempt of court. Late in the evening, the Sindh health secretary issued a notification, restoring the original eight-member medical board. Following the notification, the police surgeon sent a letter to the magistrate concerned and other members of the board, informing them that the exhumation is scheduled to be conducted at the graveyard adjacent to Rehmania Masjid at 11am on Saturday (today). Prior to the restoration of the original medical board, the police surgeon expressed her frustration over “impediments” in a post on X. The post was deleted after the government restored the eight-member board. It may be noted that the case took a new turn when the police surgeon told a private news channel on Tuesday that the post-mortem findings had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. Her interview prompted the police authorities to issue a statement, terming such observations as having the potential to adversely affect the ongoing investigation.
